736.title: Not yet
736.hook: Ananda was still unawakened when the Buddha died, and wept
736.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, a sekha or learner is a disciple who has entered the path but not completed it, and Ananda's story is told to encourage practitioners who are still on the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Prakriti, and a cup of water that birth couldn't block. Your line, I asked for water. Today, a long night for Ananda, and what he still hadn't reached.

Night, in a grove of sal trees at Kusinara. The Buddha is dying. Around him are monks of every kind: some, the texts say, fully free, and some still on the way. Ananda is among the second group. He has been at the teacher's side for many years, and kept what he heard. And he is not yet awakened. Earlier on this path we watched him slip away to weep in a doorway, and the Buddha call him back. Today, stay with the two words under the whole scene: not yet.
screen: `A GROVE AT KUSINARA.` → `SOME FREE, SOME ON THE WAY.` → `NOT YET.`

segments.voice: First, the start, long before. In the Samyutta Nikaya, Ananda remembers that when he was newly ordained, a monk named Punna taught him, and hearing it, he broke through to the teaching. So Ananda had entered the path early. On this night he wasn't a beginner. He was a learner. Second, the learner at the end. The Pali word is sekha: one still in training, on the path but not at its end. In the doorway, Ananda says it of himself, in paraphrase: I'm still a learner, with work left to do, and my teacher, who was so kind to me, is passing away. The Buddha doesn't call that failure. He tells Ananda he has served him well, and says: keep at it, and you'll soon be free. Soon. Not now. Third, the night itself. When the Buddha passes, the discourse says some monks weep and some bear it calmly: everything made comes apart. Ananda speaks a verse about the shock of that moment. And then, the text says, Anuruddha, one of the monks already free, and Ananda spent the rest of that night together, talking about the teaching. The finished one and the unfinished one, side by side until morning. Fourth, what not yet means. It isn't never. In the texts, the learner is already on the path and counted among the noble disciples. Ananda had kept what he heard, served his teacher faithfully, and still wasn't done, and the story treats that as a place to stand rather than a verdict. Tomorrow, how not yet ended.

segments.voice: Name one thing in your life that's still unfinished, a habit, a skill, a grief, and say it plainly, then add two words: not yet. Then, the way the Buddha did for Ananda, name one thing you have already done well, and hold both with the breath.
Not yet. When the Buddha died, Ananda was still a learner, on the path and not at its end, and he wept; the Buddha's word for him was soon. Today's word.
Your line: soon, not now. Not yet isn't never, and nobody sent the learner away. That's day seven hundred thirty-six.

737.title: Between standing and lying
737.hook: the night before the council, Ananda gives up striving, lies down, and is freed before his head reaches the pillow (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
737.carry: before his head reached the pillow
737.howItsDone: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions tell Ananda's last night as a story about balanced effort, and recall it for students whose practice has grown tight and forced.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not yet. The teacher had died, and Ananda wept, still a learner. Your line was soon, not now. Tonight the council is one day away.

A deadline, and a sacred one. The elders are gathering at Rajagaha to recite the teaching together, and in the Vinaya's account every one of them has already reached the end of the path. Every one except Ananda: the man who walked beside the Buddha, carried his water, heard the discourses day after day. So on the last night he does the obvious thing with a deadline. He works, attending to the body hour after hour, pushing at a door that won't open. Then, toward dawn, he stops pushing. He decides to lie down.
screen: `A COUNCIL TOMORROW.` → `EVERYONE ARRIVED BUT ONE.` → `HE PUSHES ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the push. The Vinaya says Ananda spent much of that night in mindfulness of the body. This isn't a lazy man looking for a shortcut; it's a careful one, practicing the way he was taught. And still, by effort alone, nothing gives. Second, the letting go. Toward dawn he thinks: let me lie down. He isn't quitting the path, only setting down the strain. A later commentary adds a reason: he saw that his effort had grown too tight, and he eased it. Third, the moment itself. He leans his body toward the bed, and the text says that before his head reached the pillow, while his feet had not yet left the ground, his mind was freed. Not sitting, not walking, not lying down. Somewhere in between. The thing he had chased so long came in a moment that doesn't even have a name. Fourth, what it says. Ananda didn't stop practicing; his long practice was the ground under his feet. What he stopped was the clutching. The story doesn't say effort is useless. It says effort can tighten into a fist, and a closed fist can't receive anything. In the morning, the account goes on, he took his place among the elders as one of them.
screen: `HE PUSHED ALL NIGHT.` · `HE LET GO, AND LAY DOWN.` · `BEFORE HIS HEAD TOUCHED THE PILLOW.` · `EFFORT, WITHOUT THE FIST.` · then, large: `BETWEEN STANDING AND LYING.`

segments.voice: Notice where you're pushing right now: the jaw, the shoulders, the space between the eyebrows, maybe even the breath, being managed. Let one of those go, the way Ananda let himself lie down; you're only setting down the extra, and if you catch yourself working hard at relaxing, smile at it. Then stay with the breath as it is, without trying to improve it.
Arahant. What Ananda becomes the night before the council, freed between standing and lying, before his head reaches the pillow. Today's word.
Your line: before his head reached the pillow. What he chased came when the clutching stopped. Rest easy.

738.title: The recital
738.hook: at the first council Mahakassapa asks and Ananda answers: where each discourse was spoken, and to whom (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
738.tomorrow: The couple who didn't want to marry
738.howItsDone: Monks and nuns in Theravada communities still learn discourses and verses by heart and chant them together, and the recitation of texts is a regular part of monastery life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arahant. Ananda set down the strain and was freed. Your line: before his head reached the pillow. This morning he walks into the council.

One elder asks. One elder answers. The teacher who spoke these words is gone, and a room full of elders at Rajagaha has one job: make sure what he said doesn't drift away. So the Vinaya describes something like a very calm exam. Mahakassapa, presiding, asks. Ananda answers. Everyone else listens closely, because once the answers are agreed, this is the teaching they will carry. It all rests on one man's memory, and on a room willing to check it.

First, the questions. They're about place and people before doctrine. In the Vinaya's account Kassapa asks: where was the discourse called the Net of Brahma spoken? Ananda answers: on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, at the king's rest house in Ambalatthika. And about whom? A wanderer named Suppiya and a young brahmin, his pupil. Then the next discourse, and the next, through the collections. Second, why place and people. A teaching remembered with its setting is harder to bend. If you know who was standing there and what they asked, you know what the answer was answering. It may be part of why the discourses begin with a town, a grove, a person. Third, an honest gap. Ananda also reports that near the end the Buddha told him the community could drop the lesser and minor rules after he was gone. Which ones, the elders ask. And Ananda has to say he didn't ask. They talk it over, Kassapa proposes keeping every rule as it was, and the elders agree. A good memory also remembers what it never got. Fourth, the room. Tradition says the elders chanted it back together, and from then on the teaching lived in voices: groups of monks reciting it aloud, generation after generation. One man remembered. A whole room made sure the memory held.
screen: `WHERE WAS IT SPOKEN? TO WHOM?` · `A SETTING KEEPS THE MEANING.` · `THE QUESTION HE NEVER ASKED.` · `A ROOM RECITES IT BACK.` · then, large: `HE REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Recite one verse by heart: a line from any tradition you love, or this one from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Say it slowly three or four times, out loud if you can, then close your eyes and say it without looking. Where you stumble, look once and try again, and when it holds, let it go quiet and rest with the breath.
The recital. At the first council Kassapa asks where each discourse was spoken and to whom, and Ananda answers from memory. Today's word.
Your line: he remembered. A setting keeps the meaning from bending. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.

739.title: The couple who didn't want to marry
739.hook: Pippali and Bhadda, both longing to leave the household life, are married anyway and live as friends (commentary on AN 1.14)
739.howItsDone: The story of Pippali and Bhadda is told in the Theravada commentaries as the early life of Mahakassapa and Bhadda Kapilani.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the recital. Kassapa asked, Ananda answered, and your line was he remembered. Today we meet the elder who asked the questions, long before he was an elder.

A young man in a rich brahmin family is told it's time to marry. He doesn't want to; he wants to leave home for the holy life. His parents keep pressing, so, the commentary says, he tries a clever way out. He has a statue of a woman made in gold, and announces he'll marry only someone who looks like that. Surely no such woman exists. The family's messengers carry the statue from town to town, and in a town called Sagala, they find her. Her name is Bhadda. And she doesn't want to marry either.
screen: `A SON WHO WON'T MARRY.` → `A GOLDEN STATUE.` → `THEY FIND HER ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: This is the story the commentaries tell of Pippali, who will become Mahakassapa, and Bhadda Kapilani. First, the letters. Each writes to the other: I hear we're to be married; find someone else; I mean to leave home. The story says the letters were stopped on the road and swapped for warmer ones, so the families got their wedding. Second, the wedding night. They talk, and find they want the same thing, so they agree to live as companions, not as husband and wife. A garland of flowers lies on the bed between them, and the story says neither crossed it. Third, the long friendship. They run a large estate together and stay friends. The tradition doesn't present this as sad or cold; it presents two people who understood each other and kept faith with what they'd agreed. Fourth, the turn. One day, the story goes, Pippali watches birds eating the worms turned up by his plows, and Bhadda watches crows eating insects in the seeds laid out to dry. Each feels the weight of the harm their wealth depends on. So they shave their heads, put on simple robes, take up clay bowls, and walk out of the house together, while the people of the estate weep at the door. Where they went from there is a story for another day.
screen: `TWO LETTERS, SWAPPED ON THE ROAD.` · `A GARLAND BETWEEN THEM.` · `FRIENDS WHO RUN AN ESTATE.` · `THEY WALK OUT TOGETHER.` · then, large: `TWO WHO WANTED TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a couple you know, your own if you have one, or your parents, friends or grandparents, and look past the roles, the bills and the schedule for the friendship underneath. Find one moment when they were clearly on the same side, and hold it for a while. If it's your own partnership, think of one thing you could say that a friend would say, then rest with the breath.
Nekkhamma, renunciation. What Pippali and Bhadda both longed for, even though they married, until they walked out of their house together. Today's word.
Your line: two who wanted to leave. They waited, side by side, until they could. See you tomorrow.

740.title: Exchanging robes
740.hook: the Buddha gives Kassapa his worn rag robes and takes Kassapa's soft patchwork cloak (SN 16.11)
740.howItsDone: In some Theravada forest monasteries monks still sew robes from donated or cast-off cloth and dye them by hand, and the story of the exchanged robes is told as the bond between the Buddha and Mahakassapa.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nekkhamma. Pippali and Bhadda, two who wanted to leave, walked out of their house together. Today Pippali meets his teacher.

Years later, an old monk tells Ananda about the day he met the Buddha. He's not in a sentimental mood; he's making a point. But the story is tender anyway. He'd left home, he says, already wearing a robe, and set out looking for a teacher. On the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, at a shrine by the way, he saw the Buddha sitting, and knew at once: this is my teacher. What happened next involved two pieces of cloth.
screen: `AN OLD MONK REMEMBERS.` → `A SHRINE BY THE ROAD.` → `THIS IS MY TEACHER.`

segments.voice: First, the seat. In the discourse, Kassapa bows and declares himself the Buddha's disciple. They walk on together, and the Buddha steps off the road to sit at the foot of a tree. Kassapa folds his own outer robe, a patchwork cloak, and lays it down as a seat. Second, the remark. The Buddha sits and says, in effect: this patchwork cloak of yours is soft. That's all, a comment about cloth. Kassapa hears what's underneath it and offers the cloak as a gift. Third, the exchange. The Buddha accepts, and asks a question back: will you wear my rag robes, the worn-out hempen ones? These are robes made from cloth other people threw away. Kassapa says yes. The teacher takes the soft cloak; the student takes the rough, worn one. Fourth, what Kassapa makes of it. Telling the story to Ananda, he says that if anyone could rightly be called the Buddha's true son, heir to his worn rag robes, it would be him. Not heir to a throne or a teaching hall. Heir to his old clothes. Kassapa treasured the worn one because of whose it had been, and what it said: a life with few wants, chosen on purpose.

Notice what that stirs up, and rest with the breath.

Your line: the worn robe. The soft cloak is the easy thing to want. Day seven hundred forty.

741.title: The strict practices
741.hook: rag robes, alms food, living in the forest: the Buddha tells Kassapa he is old and may let them go, and Kassapa explains why he keeps them (SN 16.5)
741.howItsDone: In the Thai forest tradition and other Theravada communities, some monks take up dhutanga practices for a time or for life, such as eating one meal a day from the alms round or living in the forest, while others keep only the ordinary rules.

segments.voice: Yesterday: exchanging robes. Kassapa gave his soft cloak and took the Buddha's worn rag robes. Your line was the worn robe. Today, how long he kept wearing it.

The robes are heavy now. That's the first thing the Buddha says in this short discourse. Kassapa has grown old, and the hempen rag robes he's worn so long hang heavy on him. So the Buddha makes a kind offer: you're old, Kassapa. Wear the robes householders give you, accept meals when people invite you, and live near me instead of out in the forest. Nobody would blame him; his teacher is giving permission. And Kassapa, politely, says no.
screen: `THE ROBES ARE HEAVY NOW.` → `A KIND OFFER.` → `KASSAPA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, what he keeps. Kassapa lists his way of life: a long time in the forest, eating only alms food, wearing rag robes, keeping only the robes he needs, wanting little, content, secluded, putting in effort. And he praises these things to others too. Later tradition gathers practices like these under one name, dhutanga. Second, the name. In the Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa's long handbook, they're explained as practices of a monk who has shaken off the defilements. They're not required of anyone. They're chosen, on top of the ordinary rules, by those who want a sharper, simpler life. Third, his reasons. The Buddha asks why he keeps them, and Kassapa gives two. One: they make a pleasant life for him, here and now. He isn't suffering through them; he likes living this way. Two: compassion for those who come later. He hopes people in the future will say, the Buddha's disciples lived like this, and take heart, and try it too. Fourth, the answer. The Buddha says: good, good, Kassapa. You're practicing for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world. So an old man keeps carrying heavy robes, not to prove anything, but so someone he'll never meet can see the path is still walked.
screen: `FOREST, ALMS, RAG ROBES.` · `PRACTICES OF SHAKING OFF.` · `A PLEASANT LIFE, HERE AND NOW.` · `AN EXAMPLE FOR LATER PEOPLE.` · then, large: `FOR THOSE TO COME.`

segments.voice: Think of one small, plain habit you keep or once kept: a walk without the phone, tea without a screen, one meal eaten slowly. Ask Kassapa's two questions about it: does it make this life a little more pleasant, here and now, and who might see it, a child, a roommate, a friend, and quietly take it up? No big answer is needed; then rest with the breath.
Dhutanga. Simple, strict practices, like forest living, alms food and rag robes, taken up by choice; Kassapa keeps them into old age. Today's word.
Your line: for those to come. A simple life can be a gift to people you'll never meet. Day seven hundred forty-one, done.

chat.says: If the Buddha said Kassapa could ease up, why keep the hard practices?
options: He liked living that way, and hoped it would encourage people who came later.
He thought the offer was a test, and refusing it would prove his worth.
He believed that without them he would lose his awakening.
chat.meaning: Kassapa gave two reasons: a pleasant life here and now, and compassion for those to come. The Buddha answered: good, good, Kassapa.

742.title: The leper's offering
742.hook: on his alms round Kassapa stands by a man with leprosy, accepts a lump of rice from his hand, and eats it (Theragatha, Mahakassapa's verses)
742.howItsDone: On the alms round in Theravada countries, monks walk in silence and receive whatever food is placed in the bowl, from any householder; Kassapa's verses about the leper's rice are one of the texts that show this way of receiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhutanga, the strict practices Kassapa kept into old age. Your line: for those to come. Today, one of his alms rounds.

Morning, and an old monk walks into town with his bowl. This is the alms round: you don't choose the food, and you don't choose the giver. You stand, and you receive what's offered. Today the one who wants to give is a man with leprosy, sitting and eating his own meal. Kassapa doesn't cross the street. He goes and stands beside him, and the man lifts a lump of rice in his damaged hand and puts it in the bowl. These lines are Kassapa's own, in the verses the tradition gives him.
screen: `A BOWL, A MORNING ROUND.` → `HE STANDS BESIDE HIM.` → `RICE FROM A DAMAGED HAND.`

segments.voice: First, the offering. In the verses, the man's hand is so damaged by his illness that, as he places the food in the bowl, a finger falls in with it. The poem doesn't look away from that. Second, the eating. Kassapa says he sat down by a wall and ate that rice, and he adds the line that gives the story its force: while eating, and afterward, he felt no disgust. Third, why he tells it. These aren't boasting verses. They sit among lines about a simple life: food from the alms round, medicine from what others discard, a seat at the foot of a tree. For Kassapa, a gift is a gift, and the giver isn't graded first. The man with leprosy got to do what the other householders did: give, and be received. Fourth, what it isn't. The story isn't asking anyone to ignore illness or take risks with health. It's about what comes after a gift is taken: the quiet recoil, the polite thanks, the thing set aside later. The verses say none of that came. And this closes a week of great disciples: Ananda's tears and his night as arahant, the recital, Pippali and Bhadda leaving together, the worn robe, the strict practices, and now a lump of rice from an unexpected hand.
screen: `A GIFT FROM A DAMAGED HAND.` · `HE ATE, AND FELT NO DISGUST.` · `THE GIVER ISN'T GRADED FIRST.` · `NO RECOIL, DURING OR AFTER.` · then, large: `HE ATE IT.`

segments.voice: Think of a gift you accepted politely and quietly set aside: a clumsy present still in its box, advice you nodded at, a dish you praised and didn't finish. Ask what was actually offered, and what it would take to use it, the way Kassapa ate the rice. Let yourself receive it fully now, and if thanks come up, let them come.
Dana, giving. What the man with leprosy offers Kassapa on his alms round, rice from a damaged hand, received and eaten without disgust. Today's word.
Your line: he ate it. He didn't only accept the gift; he received it all the way. That's day seven hundred forty-two.

fork.setup: you're on your alms round. a man with leprosy wants to give you rice from his own hand. what do you do?
options: walk on to the next house.
stand beside him and receive it.
accept it, then leave it uneaten.
fork.reveal: Kassapa stands by him, receives the rice, sits down by a wall and eats it, feeling no disgust.

original.note: Pali dana, giving: the man's offering is dana, received like any other.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a monk proving he was tough.
what it means: a gift is received all the way through, eaten and not set aside, with no disgust during or after.
what a scholar hears: the scene is in Mahakassapa's own verses in the Theragatha, set among lines about the simple needs of a monk.
recall: the invitation to point out faults

chat.says: Why does it matter that Kassapa actually ate the man's rice?
options: Because he received the gift fully, with no recoil, not just politely.
Because it proved monks can't catch any illness at all.
Because the story says caring for your health doesn't matter.
chat.meaning: In his verses Kassapa ate the rice and felt no disgust, during or after. The giver wasn't graded first; the gift was truly received.
